graph_metadata.title: Bitcoin — Full Detail Knowledge Graph
graph_metadata.description: Comprehensive machine-readable graph of Bitcoin's history, cryptographic primitives, UTXO transaction model, proof-of-work mining, consensus, Bitcoin Core C++ implementation context, wallets, scaling, privacy, economics, governance, and legal/ecological issues, based on the supplied article plus clearly labeled explanatory modeling.
graph_metadata.source_basis: User-supplied Wikipedia article text with explanatory modeling and an explicit C-versus-C++ implementation clarification.

entities.name: Bitcoin
entities.description: Decentralized peer-to-peer digital currency and payment system introduced in 2008–2009; uses a public blockchain and proof-of-work consensus.

entities.name: Bitcoin peer-to-peer network
entities.description: Global peer-to-peer network through which nodes relay transactions and blocks without a central administrator.

entities.name: Bitcoin Core
entities.description: Major open-source reference implementation of the Bitcoin protocol; the supplied article identifies it as the implementation and says it is written in C++.

entities.name: C++
entities.description: Primary implementation language of Bitcoin Core according to the supplied article; C++ is related to but distinct from C.

entities.name: C programming language
entities.description: Procedural systems programming language. Bitcoin Core is not accurately described as being written in C; it is written in C++.

entities.name: Free and open-source software
entities.description: Software whose source code is available under its license for inspection, modification, and redistribution.

entities.name: MIT License
entities.description: Permissive open-source license listed in the supplied article for Bitcoin Core.

entities.name: Satoshi Nakamoto
entities.description: Pseudonym of the unknown author of the Bitcoin white paper and original implementation.

entities.name: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
entities.description: White paper posted to a cryptography mailing list on 31 October 2008.

entities.name: bitcoin.org
entities.description: Domain registered on 18 August 2008; early project website.

entities.name: Genesis block
entities.description: First block in the Bitcoin blockchain, mined on 3 January 2009.

entities.name: The Times headline embedded in genesis block
entities.description: Text embedded in the genesis block: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks'.

entities.name: Hal Finney
entities.description: Cryptographer and early Bitcoin participant who received the first described Bitcoin transaction from Nakamoto.

entities.name: Wei Dai
entities.description: Cryptographer who proposed b-money in 1998, a conceptual precursor to Bitcoin.

entities.name: Nick Szabo
entities.description: Researcher who proposed bit gold in 1998, a conceptual precursor to Bitcoin.

entities.name: David Chaum
entities.description: Creator associated with ecash, an earlier digital-cash system developed in the 1980s.

entities.name: Cynthia Dwork
entities.description: Researcher who, with Moni Naor, proposed computational puzzles as a way to price or deter junk mail.

entities.name: Moni Naor
entities.description: Researcher who, with Cynthia Dwork, proposed computational puzzles as a way to price or deter junk mail.

entities.name: Adam Back
entities.description: Cryptographer who developed Hashcash, a proof-of-work scheme for spam control in 1997.

entities.name: Hashcash
entities.description: Proof-of-work scheme developed for spam control; a conceptual antecedent to Bitcoin mining.

entities.name: Reusable proof of work (RPOW)
entities.description: Reusable proof-of-work currency system developed by Hal Finney in 2004.

entities.name: Martti Malmi
entities.description: Finnish developer and early Bitcoin contributor who helped create content for bitcoin.org.

entities.name: Gavin Andresen
entities.description: Early developer who received network alert-key and code-repository control from Nakamoto, according to the supplied article.

entities.name: Arvind Narayanan
entities.description: Computer scientist cited in the article for analysis of Bitcoin's academic and technical antecedents.

entities.name: Bitcoin blockchain
entities.description: Ordered public ledger of transactions represented as blocks linked through cryptographic hashes.

entities.name: Block
entities.description: Container of transactions plus metadata including a header and a reference to the preceding block.

entities.name: Block header
entities.description: Block metadata hashed for proof of work; includes fields such as previous-block hash, timestamp, target encoding, and nonce.

entities.name: Previous-block hash
entities.description: Hash reference linking a block to its predecessor and making history tampering computationally costly.

entities.name: Bitcoin transaction
entities.description: Signed instruction that spends existing unspent transaction outputs and creates new outputs.

entities.name: Transaction input
entities.description: Reference to a previous unspent transaction output being spent.

entities.name: Transaction output
entities.description: Amount of bitcoin locked by a script that specifies conditions for spending.

entities.name: Unspent transaction output (UTXO)
entities.description: Output created by a transaction that has not yet been spent; the basic spendable unit tracked by Bitcoin nodes.

entities.name: UTXO set
entities.description: Set of currently unspent outputs used to determine whether transaction inputs are spendable.

entities.name: Bitcoin address
entities.description: Human-shareable encoding used to direct funds; often derived from a public key or represents a script condition.

entities.name: Private key
entities.description: Secret scalar used to authorize spending by producing digital signatures; loss can permanently remove access to funds.

entities.name: Public key
entities.description: Public cryptographic value corresponding to a private key and used in signature verification or address/script constructions.

entities.name: Digital signature
entities.description: Cryptographic proof authorizing a transaction under a relevant spending condition.

entities.name: ECDSA
entities.description: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm historically used by Bitcoin for signatures.

entities.name: Schnorr signatures
entities.description: Signature scheme enabled for Bitcoin through Taproot, with functionality benefits including improved signature handling.

entities.name: Elliptic-curve cryptography
entities.description: Public-key cryptography used in Bitcoin key and signature operations.

entities.name: Cryptographic hash function
entities.description: Deterministic function mapping data to a fixed-size digest, used in block linking, proof of work, and other protocol operations.

entities.name: SHA-256
entities.description: Hash algorithm used twice on Bitcoin block headers for proof-of-work and block identifiers.

entities.name: Double SHA-256
entities.description: Application of SHA-256 twice, used for Bitcoin block-header hashing.

entities.name: Nonce
entities.description: Variable miners change while searching for a block header hash below the difficulty target.

entities.name: Proof-of-work difficulty target
entities.description: Numerical threshold that a candidate block hash must be below to satisfy proof of work.

entities.name: Proof of work
entities.description: Computational puzzle mechanism used to make block production costly and establish a chain with accumulated work.

entities.name: Bitcoin mining
entities.description: Process of selecting and assembling transactions, searching for valid proof of work, and proposing candidate blocks.

entities.name: Bitcoin miner
entities.description: Participant that constructs candidate blocks and expends computation searching for a valid proof of work.

entities.name: Hash rate
entities.description: Rate at which mining hardware computes candidate hashes.

entities.name: Mining hardware
entities.description: Computers used to perform proof-of-work calculations; modern mining uses specialized equipment.

entities.name: Application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC)
entities.description: Specialized mining hardware designed to perform hashing efficiently.

entities.name: Graphics processing unit (GPU)
entities.description: Parallel processor that has been used for mining, though specialized ASICs dominate Bitcoin proof-of-work.

entities.name: Field-programmable gate array (FPGA)
entities.description: Reconfigurable hardware historically used for cryptocurrency mining.

entities.name: Mining pool
entities.description: Group of miners coordinating work and sharing rewards to reduce payout variance; can concentrate hash power.

entities.name: Coinbase transaction
entities.description: Special first transaction in a block that claims the block subsidy and collected transaction fees.

entities.name: Block subsidy
entities.description: Newly issued bitcoin claimable by a valid block's coinbase transaction.

entities.name: Block reward
entities.description: Miner compensation consisting of the block subsidy plus transaction fees.

entities.name: Bitcoin halving
entities.description: Scheduled reduction of the block subsidy by half every 210,000 blocks.

entities.name: Transaction fee
entities.description: Difference between total transaction inputs and outputs; paid to the miner of a block including the transaction.

entities.name: Difficulty adjustment
entities.description: Protocol recalculation every 2,016 blocks to keep average block interval near ten minutes.

entities.name: Ten-minute target block interval
entities.description: Target average interval between blocks, not a guaranteed exact interval.

entities.name: Bitcoin node
entities.description: Software participant that independently checks transactions and blocks and maintains ledger state.

entities.name: Full node
entities.description: Node that validates consensus rules and maintains blockchain/UTXO data needed for independent verification.

entities.name: Lightweight wallet/client
entities.description: Client that sends and receives transactions without storing and validating the entire blockchain locally.

entities.name: Simplified payment verification (SPV)
entities.description: Lightweight verification approach that relies on block headers and proofs rather than a complete locally validated chain.

entities.name: Blockchain explorer
entities.description: Tool for viewing public block, transaction, and address-related data.

entities.name: Bitcoin consensus
entities.description: Convergence of independently validating nodes on the valid chain with the greatest accumulated proof of work.

entities.name: Accumulated chain work
entities.description: Cumulative proof-of-work measure used to compare competing valid chains; often simplified as the most-work chain rather than merely longest by block count.

entities.name: Most-work chain selection
entities.description: Nodes follow the valid chain with the greatest accumulated work; commonly described informally as the longest-chain rule.

entities.name: Double spending
entities.description: Attempt to spend the same value more than once by creating conflicting transactions.

entities.name: Majority hash-rate attack
entities.description: Attack in which an adversary controlling a majority of hash rate may reorganize recent history, censor transactions, or double-spend; it does not permit arbitrary rule violations.

entities.name: Sybil attack
entities.description: Attack in which one actor creates many apparent identities; proof of work helps make influence depend on computational work rather than node count.

entities.name: Byzantine fault tolerance
entities.description: Ability to maintain agreement despite some adversarial or faulty participants, under the protocol's assumptions.

entities.name: Transaction validation
entities.description: Checks that transactions satisfy consensus rules, including valid inputs, signatures/scripts, and no spending of unavailable outputs.

entities.name: Block validation
entities.description: Checks that a proposed block and its transactions satisfy consensus rules, including proof of work and valid transaction ordering/state transitions.

entities.name: Mempool
entities.description: Node-local collection of valid-looking unconfirmed transactions waiting for inclusion in a block; mempools can differ among nodes.

entities.name: Peer-to-peer relay
entities.description: Propagation of transactions and blocks among connected nodes.

entities.name: Blockchain fork
entities.description: Divergence in block histories or software rules; temporary chain splits can resolve, while consensus-rule splits may persist.

entities.name: Soft fork
entities.description: Backward-compatible tightening of consensus rules for nodes that do not upgrade in certain respects.

entities.name: Hard fork
entities.description: Change not compatible with older consensus rules, potentially creating a persistent separate chain.

entities.name: Segregated Witness (SegWit)
entities.description: 2017 upgrade that changed transaction data accounting and signature-data handling, supporting capacity improvements and Lightning Network use.

entities.name: Taproot
entities.description: Upgrade activated in November 2021 adding Schnorr signatures and improved scripting/privacy-efficiency capabilities.

entities.name: Bitcoin Cash
entities.description: Separate cryptocurrency created in 2017 after a dispute over scaling and block-size policy.

entities.name: Lightning Network
entities.description: Second-layer payment network designed to enable faster, lower-on-chain-footprint Bitcoin payments through payment channels.

entities.name: Payment channel
entities.description: Mechanism allowing parties to update payment balances off-chain and settle opening/closing state on the base chain.

entities.name: Bitcoin scalability
entities.description: Ability to process more transactions while preserving acceptable cost, latency, and decentralization.

entities.name: Block-size and block-weight constraints
entities.description: Constraints on block capacity that limit base-layer transaction throughput and can affect fees and confirmation delays.

entities.name: Bitcoin privacy
entities.description: Degree to which transaction activity can be linked to people; Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not inherently anonymous.

entities.name: Pseudonymity
entities.description: Transactions refer to addresses rather than directly to civil identities, while all on-chain activity remains publicly observable.

entities.name: Fungibility
entities.description: Interchangeability of units; Bitcoin protocol treats units under the same rules, but transaction histories may lead third parties to discriminate.

entities.name: Blockchain chain analysis
entities.description: Analysis of public transaction graph and usage patterns to infer address relationships or likely identities.

entities.name: Address reuse avoidance
entities.description: Generating new receiving addresses can reduce some linkability but does not guarantee anonymity.

entities.name: Bitcoin wallet
entities.description: Software or device managing keys and transaction data needed to receive, construct, sign, and broadcast bitcoin transactions; it does not literally store coins.

entities.name: Hot wallet
entities.description: Wallet whose keys or signing capability are connected to an internet-connected system, creating online compromise risks.

entities.name: Cold storage
entities.description: Keeping private keys offline to reduce exposure to online attacks.

entities.name: Hardware wallet
entities.description: Dedicated device that protects private keys and signs transactions while limiting key exposure to a general-purpose computer.

entities.name: Paper wallet
entities.description: Printed key material or recovery information; vulnerable to loss, damage, theft, and unsafe generation practices.

entities.name: Custodial wallet
entities.description: Service in which a third party controls the keys or credentials associated with users' funds.

entities.name: Non-custodial wallet
entities.description: Wallet where the user controls the private keys or signing authority.

entities.name: Multisignature script
entities.description: Spending condition requiring signatures from multiple distinct keys according to a configured threshold or policy.

entities.name: Bitcoin Script
entities.description: Forth-like stack-based scripting language used to express transaction output spending conditions.

entities.name: Script hash
entities.description: Hash-based representation used in certain address formats to commit to spending conditions.

entities.name: Satoshi
entities.description: Smallest base unit described in the article: one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin.

entities.name: Millibitcoin (mBTC)
entities.description: One-thousandth of a bitcoin.

entities.name: Microbitcoin
entities.description: One-millionth of a bitcoin.

entities.name: BTC
entities.description: Common code for bitcoin; article notes that XBT is also used in some contexts.

entities.name: XBT
entities.description: Code used by some financial data services; conforms to the X-prefixed convention but is not officially recognized by ISO according to the article.

entities.name: Bitcoin sign ₿
entities.description: Unicode character U+20BF commonly used as Bitcoin's symbol.

entities.name: 21-million bitcoin supply limit
entities.description: Protocol issuance limit commonly described as 21 million bitcoin; exact theoretical total is slightly below 21 million due to subsidy schedule rounding.

entities.name: Bitcoin issuance schedule
entities.description: Decentralized issuance through coinbase block subsidies that halve every 210,000 blocks.

entities.name: Circulating bitcoin supply
entities.description: Amount of bitcoin considered in circulation at a given date; estimates are date-sensitive.

entities.name: Floating exchange rate
entities.description: Bitcoin's price is market-determined and can vary significantly across time and venues.

entities.name: Price volatility
entities.description: Large and sometimes rapid price changes that affect bitcoin's suitability for pricing and everyday payments.

entities.name: Cryptocurrency exchange
entities.description: Service or marketplace where users trade bitcoin for fiat currencies or other digital assets.

entities.name: Bitcoin futures
entities.description: Derivative contracts giving exposure to bitcoin prices; CME futures began in December 2017 according to the article.

entities.name: Spot bitcoin exchange-traded fund
entities.description: Exchange-traded investment product designed to provide exposure to spot bitcoin prices; US spot products began trading in January 2024 according to the article.

entities.name: Bitcoin as an investment asset
entities.description: Use of bitcoin as a speculative investment or store-of-value claim rather than primarily for routine payments.

entities.name: Store of value
entities.description: Function of an asset to preserve purchasing power over time; Bitcoin's performance in this role is contested.

entities.name: Medium of exchange
entities.description: Function of money used to buy goods or services; bitcoin usage is constrained by volatility, fees, and confirmation latency.

entities.name: Unit of account
entities.description: Function of money as a common denomination for quoting prices; prices are rarely denominated directly in bitcoin according to the article.

entities.name: Austrian school of economics
entities.description: Economic tradition associated in the article with Bitcoin's ideological roots and free-market monetary ideas.

entities.name: Friedrich Hayek
entities.description: Economist whose book The Denationalisation of Money argued for competition in money production and management.

entities.name: The Denationalisation of Money
entities.description: Hayek's work cited as an ideological antecedent for private and market-based money.

entities.name: Libertarian political philosophy
entities.description: Ideological current that values individual liberty and limits on state control; some early Bitcoin proponents were attracted to it.

entities.name: Cypherpunk movement
entities.description: Community promoting privacy-enhancing cryptography and technologies for individual autonomy; contextual predecessor to Bitcoin.

entities.name: Bitcoin regulation
entities.description: Legal and compliance treatment of Bitcoin, exchanges, miners, and intermediaries varies by jurisdiction.

entities.name: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)
entities.description: US agency that issued 2013 guidance on decentralized virtual currencies and certain money-services obligations.

entities.name: Legal tender status
entities.description: Legal designation for a currency or payment instrument; Bitcoin's status varies by jurisdiction and over time.

entities.name: El Salvador
entities.description: Country that adopted bitcoin as legal tender in 2021 alongside the US dollar, followed by a 2025 reform removing mandatory acceptance obligations according to the supplied article.

entities.name: Central African Republic
entities.description: Country that adopted bitcoin as legal tender in 2022 and repealed the reform in 2023 according to the article.

entities.name: Silk Road
entities.description: Dark-web marketplace that accepted bitcoin and became an early high-profile example of its use in illicit markets.

entities.name: Mt. Gox
entities.description: Early major bitcoin exchange associated with regulatory action and large-scale losses/theft.

entities.name: Bitcoin Pizza Day
entities.description: Commemorates the 22 May 2010 purchase of two pizzas for 10,000 BTC by Laszlo Hanyecz.

entities.name: Laszlo Hanyecz
entities.description: Programmer associated with the first known commercial Bitcoin purchase described in the article: two pizzas for 10,000 BTC.

entities.name: MicroStrategy / Strategy
entities.description: Company described in the article as having purchased bitcoin as a treasury reserve asset in 2020.

entities.name: Square, Inc.
entities.description: Company that purchased bitcoin in 2020 according to the article; later known as Block, Inc.

entities.name: MassMutual
entities.description: Insurer that invested in bitcoin in 2020 according to the article.

entities.name: PayPal
entities.description: Payments company that added US support for buying, holding, and selling bitcoin in November 2020 according to the article.

entities.name: BlackRock
entities.description: Asset manager discussed in the article in connection with a 2024 recommendation about possible portfolio allocation to bitcoin.

entities.name: ProShares BITO
entities.description: Bitcoin futures ETF listed in October 2021 according to the article.

entities.name: Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME)
entities.description: Exchange that introduced bitcoin futures in December 2017 and listed the ProShares BITO futures ETF.

entities.name: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
entities.description: International organization that urged El Salvador in 2022 to reverse its bitcoin legal-tender decision; the article links later reforms to IMF loan conditions.

entities.name: Environmental impact of mining
entities.description: Electricity use and electronic waste associated with proof-of-work mining; estimates and implications are debated.

entities.name: Mining electricity consumption
entities.description: Electricity used by mining hardware to compute proof of work.

entities.name: Mining electronic waste
entities.description: Discarded mining hardware resulting from short equipment lifetimes and rapid efficiency competition.

entities.name: Mining electricity energy mix
entities.description: Mix of fossil and non-fossil energy sources used by mining operations.

entities.name: 51% hash-rate threshold
entities.description: Common shorthand for majority control of active mining hash rate; can enable reorganization/censorship but cannot make invalid transactions valid to honest nodes.

entities.name: Transaction confirmation
entities.description: Inclusion of a transaction in a block; later blocks add depth and generally increase the cost of reversing it.

entities.name: Chain reorganization
entities.description: Replacement of a node's previously preferred chain with another valid chain having greater accumulated work.

entities.name: Network partition
entities.description: Temporary loss of connectivity that can cause nodes to see competing candidate chains.

entities.name: Stale/orphaned block
entities.description: Valid block not retained in the ultimately preferred chain after competing blocks are resolved.

entities.name: Transaction malleability
entities.description: Potential change in transaction identifier representation without changing the economic intent; SegWit altered relevant transaction-data handling.

entities.name: Taproot script-path spending
entities.description: Taproot spending path allowing a committed script condition to be revealed and executed when used.

entities.name: Ordinals
entities.description: Protocol convention introduced in 2023 for identifying satoshis and associating data with them, described by the article in connection with Bitcoin NFTs.

entities.name: Non-fungible token (NFT)
entities.description: Unique or non-interchangeable digital-asset representation; Ordinals enabled NFT-like uses on Bitcoin.

entities.name: Bitcoin payment processor
entities.description: Intermediary that may convert between bitcoin and fiat or facilitate merchant payments.

entities.name: Cross-border remittance
entities.description: Cross-border money transfer use case sometimes proposed for bitcoin, though article reports limited evidence of broad remittance use in 2015.

entities.name: Criminal use and illicit finance
entities.description: Illicit uses that have attracted law-enforcement and regulatory attention; Bitcoin's public ledger also enables tracing.

entities.name: Traditional account-based ledger
entities.description: Conventional ledger model contrasted with Bitcoin's model of transaction outputs and cryptographic ownership authorization.

entities.name: Peer-to-peer architecture
entities.description: System architecture in which participants communicate directly without a required central server or administrator.

entities.name: Distributed system
entities.description: Multiple independent computers coordinate over a network while maintaining state and applying common rules.

entities.name: Cryptography
entities.description: Mathematical techniques used in Bitcoin for signatures, hashes, key control, and transaction authorization.

entities.name: Digital scarcity
entities.description: Property of making digitally represented units scarce under agreed protocol rules, despite digital data being easy to copy.

entities.name: Censorship resistance
entities.description: Resistance to an actor preventing valid transactions from being relayed or included; depends on network and mining decentralization.

entities.name: Decentralization
entities.description: Distribution of validation, mining, development, custody, and infrastructure across independent actors.

entities.name: Bitcoin protocol governance
entities.description: Informal coordination among developers, node operators, miners, businesses, and users around software and consensus changes.

entities.name: Bitcoin Core developer
entities.description: Contributor who proposes, reviews, implements, or maintains Bitcoin software changes.

entities.name: Bitcoin Core release
entities.description: Versioned distribution of Bitcoin Core; article lists release 31.1.0 on 7 July 2026.

entities.name: Coin selection / coin control
entities.description: Wallet function for choosing which UTXOs to spend, affecting fees and privacy.

entities.name: Change output
entities.description: Output returning the excess value of selected inputs to the spender.

entities.name: Fee rate
entities.description: Fee expressed relative to transaction data size, commonly in satoshis per virtual byte under modern transaction accounting.

entities.name: Block subsidy schedule
entities.description: Schedule beginning at 50 BTC per block and halving every 210,000 blocks.

entities.name: Bitcoin 0.1.0
entities.description: Initial Bitcoin software release dated 9 January 2009 in the supplied article.

entities.name: Bitcoin's 2008 proposal
entities.description: Publication of Nakamoto's white paper on 31 October 2008.

entities.name: Bitcoin network launch
entities.description: Creation of the Bitcoin network through mining of the genesis block on 3 January 2009.

entities.name: First described Bitcoin transaction
entities.description: Hal Finney received 10 BTC from Nakamoto on 12 January 2009 according to the article.

entities.name: SegWit activation (2017)
entities.description: SegWit activated in August 2017.

entities.name: Taproot activation (2021)
entities.description: Taproot activated in November 2021.

entities.name: US spot bitcoin ETF launch (2024)
entities.description: First 11 US spot bitcoin ETFs began trading in January 2024 according to the article.

entities.name: Bitcoin issuance
entities.description: Creation of new bitcoin via valid coinbase subsidy claims according to consensus rules.

entities.name: Wallet backup and recovery material
entities.description: Backup of private keys, seed phrases, or other recovery data; losing all valid key material can make funds inaccessible.

entities.name: Wallet seed phrase
entities.description: Human-readable representation of wallet recovery entropy in many wallet systems; not specified as a protocol primitive in the supplied article but relevant to wallet operation.

entities.name: Economic bubble debate
entities.description: Debate over whether bitcoin price reflects sustainable value or speculative narratives and market dynamics.

entities.name: Market liquidity
entities.description: Ability to buy or sell without large price impact; varies by venue and conditions.

entities.name: Fiat currency
entities.description: Government-issued currency such as the US dollar, often used as a pricing reference and exchange pair for bitcoin.

entities.name: United States dollar
entities.description: Fiat currency used alongside bitcoin during El Salvador's 2021 legal-tender period.

entities.name: Genesis block coinbase data
entities.description: Coinbase transaction and embedded headline in the genesis block; genesis subsidy treatment is special in Bitcoin implementation.

entities.name: Consensus rules
entities.description: Rules independently enforced by nodes for valid transactions, blocks, issuance, scripts, and proof of work.

entities.name: Candidate block template
entities.description: Proposed block contents assembled by a miner or mining pool before searching for proof of work.

entities.name: Transaction selection
entities.description: Selection of mempool transactions for a candidate block, commonly influenced by fee rate and validity.

entities.name: Hash threshold puzzle
entities.description: Mining task of finding header data whose double-SHA-256 hash is numerically below the target.

entities.name: Probabilistic settlement confidence
entities.description: Confidence in transaction settlement increases with additional valid blocks but is not absolute mathematical finality.

entities.name: Mining economic incentives
entities.description: Subsidy and transaction fees incentivize miners to expend resources and propose valid blocks.

entities.name: Block propagation
entities.description: Dissemination of newly found blocks so other nodes can validate and extend the chain.

entities.name: Proof-of-work security assumption
entities.description: Security depends in part on honest or economically aligned hash power, validation by nodes, and the cost of accumulating more work than competing chains.

entities.name: Decentralized issuance
entities.description: No central issuer chooses individual issuance; issuance follows protocol-valid block subsidy rules.

entities.name: Bitcoin monetary policy
entities.description: Protocol-defined issuance and maximum-supply schedule rather than discretionary central-bank policy.

entities.name: Bitcoin price history
entities.description: Market price history characterized by large rises and falls, influenced by demand, regulation, institutional participation, and broader market events.

entities.name: 10,000 BTC pizza purchase
entities.description: Purchase by Laszlo Hanyecz of two pizzas for 10,000 BTC on 22 May 2010.

entities.name: Genesis block timestamp
entities.description: Genesis block is dated 3 January 2009.

entities.name: 3.125 BTC block subsidy (2024–2028 era)
entities.description: The supplied article states a 3.125 BTC block reward as of 2026; technically this refers to the subsidy and excludes transaction fees.

entities.name: Exact theoretical issuance ceiling
entities.description: The article's note gives an exact total of 20,999,999.9769 BTC rather than a perfectly round 21 million.

entities.name: Cryptography mailing list
entities.description: Mailing list where the Bitcoin white paper link was posted in October 2008.

entities.name: Financial crime enforcement
entities.description: Investigations and enforcement involving exchange compliance, illicit marketplaces, and seizures of bitcoin.

entities.name: Government bitcoin seizure
entities.description: Government agencies have seized bitcoin connected to investigations, as described in the article's historical examples.

entities.name: Software fork
entities.description: A copied or modified codebase that may diverge in implementation, policy, or consensus rules.

entities.name: Bitcoin Unlimited
entities.description: Fork of Bitcoin Core mentioned in the supplied article.

entities.name: Supplied Wikipedia Bitcoin article
entities.description: User-provided Bitcoin article text used as the primary source for this graph; time-sensitive claims are treated as source-reported rather than independently verified.

entities.name: Layer-two protocol
entities.description: Protocol operating above the base blockchain to improve transaction throughput, latency, or functionality while using the base chain for settlement.

entities.name: Local storage requirement
entities.description: Disk and bandwidth resources needed by a client to store blockchain data; full nodes generally require more resources than lightweight clients.

relationships.description: Bitcoin Core is a major implementation of the Bitcoin protocol.
The supplied article specifies C++, not C.
C and C++ are related but distinct languages; calling Bitcoin Core a C program would be inaccurate.
The article lists the MIT License.
Bitcoin Core is open-source software.
The white paper was published under Nakamoto's pseudonym.
The 2008 paper described a peer-to-peer electronic cash system.
The domain was registered in August 2008 before the white paper.
The link appeared on a cryptography mailing list.
Nakamoto mined the starting block.
The genesis block is the first block of the chain.
The block contains the newspaper headline text.
The embedded text includes 3 January 2009.
Finney received 10 BTC from Nakamoto.
The described early transaction was received by Finney.
Nakamoto sent the transaction.
The date commemorates the 10,000 BTC pizza purchase.
Hanyecz made the purchase.
The purchase used bitcoin as payment.
Chaum's ecash work is an early digital-cash antecedent.
Ecash was an earlier attempt at digital cash, although it relied on centralized control.
They proposed computational puzzles to combat junk mail.
Dwork and Naor's work influenced the proof-of-work lineage.

architecture_patterns.name: Peer-to-peer independent validation
architecture_patterns.description: Nodes relay data but independently apply consensus rules instead of trusting a central server.
benefits: No central ledger administrator
Independent verification
Resistance to accepting invalid state from a single service
tradeoffs: Bandwidth, storage, and validation costs
Network partitions can temporarily produce competing views

architecture_patterns.name: UTXO transaction lifecycle
architecture_patterns.description: Bitcoin value is represented as outputs created by prior transactions and consumed by later transactions.
flow: mark inputs spent and outputs unspent
benefits: Explicit ownership conditions
Straightforward double-spend checks against current UTXO state
tradeoffs: Coin selection affects privacy and fees
Change and fee handling require wallet logic

architecture_patterns.name: Proof-of-work block production
architecture_patterns.description: Miners assemble candidate blocks and repeatedly hash header variants until the result meets the target.
flow: vary nonce and other header data
benefits: Makes block creation resource-costly
Lets nodes verify a solution cheaply
tradeoffs: High electricity and hardware expenditure
Mining-pool concentration can weaken decentralization

architecture_patterns.name: Most-accumulated-work chain selection
architecture_patterns.description: Nodes choose among valid competing histories based on accumulated proof of work.
flow: switch to the valid most-work chain when needed
benefits: Deterministic fork-choice rule from node perspective
Older history becomes more expensive to replace as work accumulates
tradeoffs: Settlement confidence is probabilistic
Recent transactions can be reversed by sufficiently powerful competing work

architecture_patterns.name: Coinbase issuance and miner compensation
architecture_patterns.description: A valid block's coinbase transaction claims the scheduled subsidy and fees from included transactions.
flow: create coinbase claim within consensus limits
benefits: Rule-based issuance without a central issuer
Economic incentive to secure the chain
tradeoffs: Subsidy declines over time
Long-term security depends increasingly on fee revenue and other economic conditions

architecture_patterns.name: Wallet key custody and signing
architecture_patterns.description: Wallets manage key material, create transactions, and produce authorization proofs while the network validates them.
flow: receive outputs locked to a script
benefits: Users can self-custody without an account administrator
Offline signing can reduce key exposure
tradeoffs: Lost keys can mean unrecoverable funds
Exposed keys can enable theft; custodial services introduce counterparty risk

architecture_patterns.name: Base-layer and second-layer scaling
architecture_patterns.description: Base-layer block capacity constraints motivate systems such as Lightning that move many payment updates off-chain.
flow: settle channel state on-chain when needed
benefits: Can reduce base-layer transaction demand
Can improve payment latency and throughput
tradeoffs: Channel liquidity and routing constraints
Not every operation is free of base-layer dependencies

architecture_patterns.name: Pseudonymous public ledger and chain analysis
architecture_patterns.description: Addresses obscure identities at the protocol layer but transaction graphs remain public and can be analyzed.
flow: associate clusters with known identities where evidence permits
benefits: Public auditability and verifiability
tradeoffs: Address reuse and transaction patterns can reveal links
New addresses do not guarantee anonymity

architecture_patterns.name: Bitcoin Core C++ implementation architecture
architecture_patterns.description: The supplied article identifies Bitcoin Core as the open-source implementation written in C++. This is a conceptual mapping of major subsystems, not a claim that the project is written in C.
flow: wallet logic manages keys and transaction construction
benefits: Modular implementation of a distributed protocol
Open-source review and independent builds
tradeoffs: Large systems codebase with security-critical edge cases
C++ semantics and project APIs matter; illustrative C pseudocode is not drop-in Bitcoin Core code

architecture_patterns.name: Protocol upgrade and ecosystem coordination
architecture_patterns.description: Consensus and software upgrades require coordination among developers, miners, node operators, wallets, and businesses.
flow: participants choose whether and when to upgrade
nodes enforce their configured consensus rules
benefits: Changes can be developed transparently
Users and operators retain independent rule-enforcement choices
tradeoffs: Coordination can be slow and contentious
Incompatible rules can cause persistent forks

derived_rules.rule: A transaction input must reference an available unspent output and satisfy its spending conditions.
derived_rules.implication: A valid signature alone is not sufficient if the referenced output is missing or already spent.

derived_rules.rule: A node independently validates blocks against consensus rules.
derived_rules.implication: A miner's block is not accepted merely because the miner found proof of work.

derived_rules.rule: A Bitcoin proof-of-work block header must hash below the current target under double SHA-256.
derived_rules.implication: The target defines the acceptable hash threshold.

derived_rules.rule: The valid chain with the greatest accumulated work is preferred over a competing valid chain.
derived_rules.implication: Block count alone is an incomplete description of fork choice.

derived_rules.rule: Difficulty is recalculated every 2,016 blocks to target an average block interval near ten minutes.
derived_rules.implication: Actual block times vary; ten minutes is a long-run target, not a timer.

derived_rules.rule: A coinbase transaction may claim only the permitted subsidy plus eligible fees.
derived_rules.implication: Nodes reject blocks that create excess value even if the block has valid proof of work.

derived_rules.rule: The block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks.
derived_rules.implication: Issuance declines over time and approaches a total below 21 million BTC.

derived_rules.rule: A bitcoin is divisible into 100,000,000 satoshis under the unit model described in the article.
derived_rules.implication: The satoshi is the smallest base unit in this model.

derived_rules.rule: Private keys must remain secret and backed up safely.
derived_rules.implication: Key exposure can enable theft; loss of all valid key material can make funds inaccessible.

derived_rules.rule: Bitcoin addresses and transaction histories are public, even though addresses do not directly state civil identities.
derived_rules.implication: Bitcoin is pseudonymous rather than inherently anonymous.

derived_rules.rule: Generating a new address can reduce some linkability but does not guarantee privacy.
derived_rules.implication: Public transaction patterns and external identity information can still connect activity.

derived_rules.rule: A majority-hash-rate attacker may reorganize recent blocks or censor transactions, but cannot force fully validating nodes to accept invalid transactions.
derived_rules.implication: Hash power does not override signature, supply, or block-validity rules.

derived_rules.rule: More confirmations generally increase the cost of reversing a transaction, but do not provide absolute mathematical finality.
derived_rules.implication: Risk tolerance and transaction value influence appropriate confirmation policy.

derived_rules.rule: Wallet software manages keys and transaction construction; bitcoin is represented on-chain as UTXOs, not stored inside the wallet application.
derived_rules.implication: A wallet backup protects key/recovery material rather than copying coins.

derived_rules.rule: The article identifies Bitcoin Core as written in C++, not C.
derived_rules.implication: C-like pseudocode can illustrate concepts but must not be mistaken for compilable Bitcoin Core source.

derived_rules.rule: A transaction's fee is the difference between its input value and output value, subject to valid transaction rules.
derived_rules.implication: A wallet must account for fee and change-output handling.

derived_rules.rule: Mining pools reduce individual payout variance but can aggregate decision-making and hash power.
derived_rules.implication: Pool concentration is a network-level risk even if many individual machines participate.

derived_rules.rule: A lightweight client does not provide the same independent full validation as a fully validating node.
derived_rules.implication: Convenience and lower resource use can entail reliance on peers or servers.

derived_rules.rule: Bitcoin's price is floating and has historically been volatile.
derived_rules.implication: Market price risk differs from the protocol's deterministic issuance schedule.

derived_rules.rule: Bitcoin's protocol-level fungibility does not prevent services from analyzing or discriminating based on transaction history.
derived_rules.implication: Technical interchangeability and market treatment are distinct properties.

derived_rules.rule: A soft fork tightens or changes rules in a way intended to remain compatible with non-upgraded nodes under defined conditions; a hard fork can be incompatible.
derived_rules.implication: Upgrade type influences coordination and chain-split risk.

derived_rules.rule: Lightning payment channels use off-chain state updates and depend on the base chain for relevant settlement operations.
derived_rules.implication: Second-layer payments reduce on-chain load but do not eliminate base-layer dependencies.

derived_rules.rule: A valid proof of work is easy to verify relative to the repeated computation required to find it.
derived_rules.implication: Nodes can cheaply check a candidate block's hash against the target.

derived_rules.rule: The 21-million figure is a rounded description; the article notes a theoretical total of 20,999,999.9769 BTC.
derived_rules.implication: Use exact-supply claims with the article's qualification.

derived_rules.rule: Legal status and compliance duties vary by jurisdiction and may change over time.
derived_rules.implication: Historical legal status should not be presented as current universal advice.

examples.title: Alice pays Bob using a UTXO
examples.scenario: Alice's wallet selects spendable outputs, creates an input referencing them, creates a payment output to Bob, optionally creates change, signs the spend, and broadcasts it.
steps: Wallet queries available UTXOs
Construct inputs and payment/change outputs
Calculate fee from input-output difference
Sign according to each input's script condition
Nodes validate and relay the transaction
A miner includes it in a valid block
caveats: The wallet does not contain the coins; the ledger tracks UTXOs.
A broadcast transaction is not yet confirmed.

examples.title: Miner finds a block
examples.scenario: A miner builds a candidate block and searches for a header hash below the current target.
steps: Select transactions from a mempool
Build a candidate block and coinbase transaction
Try nonce and other header variations
Double-hash the header with SHA-256
Check hash against target
Broadcast a successful candidate
Nodes independently validate it
caveats: Finding a valid hash is probabilistic and can require many attempts.
Other miners may find a competing block at nearly the same time.

examples.title: Two blocks appear at once
examples.scenario: Network latency leads different nodes to see competing valid blocks at the same height.
steps: Each branch is validated independently
Miners extend one or both branches
Nodes compare accumulated work
Nodes converge on the valid branch with more work
Transactions only in the losing branch may return to mempools if still valid
caveats: This is a normal possible network event, not automatically evidence of an attack.

examples.title: Multisignature treasury
examples.scenario: A script requires signatures from multiple distinct keys before funds can be spent.
steps: Create an output locked to a multisignature script
Distribute signing authority to separate key holders
Construct a transaction when spending is authorized
Collect required signatures
Nodes validate the script and input
caveats: Key loss and coordination failures can still prevent spending.

examples.title: Cold-storage signing
examples.scenario: A user keeps keys offline and transfers an unsigned or partially constructed transaction to an offline signer.
steps: Prepare transaction details on an online device
Review destination and amount on a trusted display
Sign with offline key material
Return signed transaction to an online device
Broadcast to the network
caveats: Offline custody reduces some remote risks but does not prevent all physical, supply-chain, or user-interface attacks.

examples.title: Lightning payment
examples.scenario: Two parties route a payment through payment channels rather than recording every update on the base chain.
steps: Open or use existing channel liquidity
Exchange off-chain channel updates
Route payment through channel network
Use the base chain for relevant channel settlement
caveats: Liquidity, routing, online availability, and channel management affect usability.

examples.title: Public-ledger privacy risk
examples.scenario: An address is not directly a person's name, but transaction patterns may link it to other addresses and known identities.
steps: Observe public transactions
Cluster addresses using spending patterns
Associate a cluster with an exchange or published identity
Infer links to other activity with varying confidence
caveats: Inference can be probabilistic and should not be treated as proof of identity without corroboration.

examples.title: C-like educational model of a UTXO spend
examples.scenario: Illustrative pseudocode models the logic of checking inputs and creating outputs. It is not production Bitcoin code and does not represent the full Bitcoin Script or consensus implementation.
examples.code_language: C-like pseudocode (illustrative only; Bitcoin Core is C++)
caveats: Educational simplification only: omits integer-overflow-safe arithmetic, serialization, locktime/sequence rules, script execution details, witness handling, fee policy, consensus edge cases, and implementation APIs. Never use as a consensus implementation.
steps: Use a simplified UTXO lookup to reject missing or already-spent inputs
Check spending authorization for each input
Sum input and output values
Reject outputs exceeding inputs
Treat the result only as a conceptual sketch, not full consensus validation

sources.title: Bitcoin — supplied Wikipedia article text
sources.source_basis: The attached article text supplied by the user; its history, design, mining, wallets, scaling, economics, and regulatory sections inform this graph.
sources.citation: The attached Bitcoin article begins with the article metadata and overview and continues through references and further reading.
limitations: Historical and time-sensitive figures are represented as claims reported by the supplied article, not independently verified current data.
This graph adds explanatory conceptual links and the C-versus-C++ clarification; those links are identified as explanatory modeling rather than verbatim article claims.

validation_notes: All relationship source and target IDs resolve to defined entities.
Entities and relationships are a conceptual knowledge graph, not a substitute for the Bitcoin consensus specification or source code.

notes: Primary source is the user-provided Bitcoin article text. Facts explicitly time-bound in that text (release version, circulating supply, price records, legal status, energy estimates, mining geography, and institutional holdings) must be read with their stated dates.

Implementation-language correction: the supplied article says Bitcoin Core is written in C++. C and C++ are related but distinct languages. The included C-like example is only educational pseudocode, not actual Bitcoin Core code.
Bitcoin is not a file or balance stored inside a wallet. On-chain value is tracked through UTXOs; wallets manage keys and transaction construction.
The 'longest chain' phrase is a shorthand. Consensus selection is more accurately described as the valid chain with the greatest accumulated proof of work.
Proof-of-work mining does not make invalid transactions valid. Fully validating nodes enforce consensus rules independently of miner hash power.
Bitcoin privacy is pseudonymity: the public transaction graph may support chain analysis, and new addresses do not guarantee anonymity.
Bitcoin's total issuance is commonly rounded to 21 million BTC; the supplied article gives a theoretical total of 20,999,999.9769 BTC.
Not investment, legal, tax, or cybersecurity advice. Laws, market conditions, and implementation details can change.
